Scheduling

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Scheduling assigns jobs to processing resources and orders their execution subject to resource and precedence requirements. Objectives include completion time, lateness and throughput. In single-machine sequencing with all jobs mandatory, the total processing time is constant, but order-dependent setups can still change completion time. With parallel machines, machine allocation and sequencing jointly determine the parallel-machine makespan with sequence-dependent setups.

Parallel-machine makespan with sequence-dependent setups (Cmax​=maxr​Cr​)

Words: 79
Scheduling OurBigBook.com
Partition jobs between machines and choose an ordering on each machine. Machine r has load Cr​ equal to its processing times, initial setup and internal changeovers; the completion time of all jobs is the maximum of these loads. Minimize a variable Cmax​ subject to Cr​≤Cmax​ for every machine. Branch and bound can combine machine-assignment decisions with route bounds; heuristic moves relocate jobs between machines, swap jobs, and reorder blocks. Minimizing the sum of route costs alone does not generally minimize the makespan.

Objective function (f(x))

Words: 22
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
An objective function assigns a numerical score to each admissible decision. An optimization problem seeks a feasible solution maximizing or minimizing this score.
// Target: mathematical-optimization.bigb

Project scheduling

Words: 204 Articles: 3
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
With unlimited parallel processing, a project is described by task durations and precedence constraints. A task can start only after its predecessors finish. For an acyclic precedence graph, minimizing total completion time amounts to finding a longest start-to-finish path.
// Target: mathematical-optimization.bigb

Critical path method

Words: 162 Articles: 2
Project scheduling OurBigBook.com
Add a dummy source before the initial tasks and a dummy sink after the terminal tasks. Give every arc leaving task i length τi​, its duration, with zero duration at the source. The longest path length is the minimum possible project duration. Earliest starts are obtained in topological order by tj​=maxi→j​(ti​+τi​). A longest path is a critical path.
// Target: mathematical-optimization.bigb

Project scheduling duality

Words: 100 Articles: 1
Critical path method OurBigBook.com
On the augmented precedence graph, the linear programming problem
min(tsink​−tsource​)subject totj​−ti​≥τi​
(1)
has dual max∑i→j​τi​fij​, with f≥0 a unit source-to-sink flow. Equivalently, the dual is the negative of the optimal uncapacitated minimum-cost flow value with arc costs −τi​. The flow selects a longest path, while the time variables provide a matching weak duality bound.
// Target: mathematical-optimization.bigb
Unit-flow certificate for project duration
Words: 45
Project scheduling duality OurBigBook.com
A feasible timetable with finish time T and a unit flow carried on a precedence path of total duration T certify optimality. Summing the inequalities tj​−ti​≥τi​ along that path proves every schedule needs at least T, while the timetable attains it.
// Target: computer-science.bigb

Maximum and minimum

Words: 87
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Maxima and minima are extrema of a real-valued function. A global maximum of f on its domain D is a point x∗​ with f(x)≤f(x∗​) for every x∈D; a global minimum reverses the inequality. A local extremum requires the inequality only in a neighbourhood of the point within D. In constrained optimization, D is the feasible set, so an extremum is tested relative to the constraints rather than in every ambient direction. Thus a constrained local maximum or local minimum can occur at a boundary point without being an interior critical point.

Cobb–Douglas production function (f(K,L)=AKαLβ)

Words: 99
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
For positive constants A,α,β, a Cobb–Douglas production function describes output in terms of capital K and labour L. It is homogeneous of degree α+β. Under K+wL=b with b,w>0, its unique nonnegative-input optimum is K=αb/(α+β) and L=βb/[w(α+β)], obtained by maximizing the strictly concave logarithm along the budget line. The optimized output has derivative (α+β)ϕ(b)/b, equal to its budget Lagrange multiplier. When α+β>1, the unconstrained Lagrangian supremum over the positive orthant is infinite for every finite multiplier, despite the finite constrained optimum; the global dual representation must not be presumed in this case.

Heuristic optimization

Words: 467 Articles: 6
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Heuristic optimization seeks useful feasible solutions without necessarily providing a universal approximation ratio or a polynomial worst-case guarantee. Examples are local search, simulated annealing and tabu search. A claimed approximation algorithm needs a separate proved performance guarantee.

Tabu search

Words: 61
Heuristic optimization OurBigBook.com
Tabu search keeps a short-term memory of recently reversed moves or visited attributes and prohibits them temporarily, reducing cycling in local search. It can select the best admissible neighbor even when that neighbor worsens the objective; an aspiration rule permits a tabu move when it improves the best known solution. For allocations, transfers and exchanges maintain feasibility and recent reverse transfers can be tabu.

Simulated annealing

Words: 330 Articles: 3
Heuristic optimization OurBigBook.com
For a maximization objective, simulated annealing accepts every improving proposed neighbor and accepts a worsening move of loss Δ with probability exp(−Δ/T) at temperature T>0. Decreasing the temperature reduces exploratory moves. Retain the best feasible solution seen. Finite practical cooling schedules carry no general global-optimality guarantee.

Likelihood-power annealing (πT​(θ)∝L(θ)1/T)

Words: 286 Articles: 2
Simulated annealing OurBigBook.com
To maximize a log-likelihood, use energy −ℓ and Boltzmann distribution proportional to eℓ/T=L1/T at temperature T>0. Reversing this sign favors likelihood minima and can make the probability density function nonnormalizable. For Poisson observations with total s and sample size m, with respect to dλ the normalized probability density function is
λ∼Gamma(s/T+1,m/T).
(2)
Its mean is (s+T)/m and variance (sT+T2)/m2, so it concentrates at the maximum-likelihood estimate s/m as T↓0. Cooling of equilibrium laws and convergence of a particular changing-temperature chain are different statements; the latter requires mixing or a direct chain argument.
Binomial likelihood-power annealing (p∼Beta(s/T+1,mn/T−s/T+1))
Words: 59
Likelihood-power annealing OurBigBook.com
For m independent binomial distribution observations with fixed trial count n and total successes s, the likelihood-power probability density function relative to dp is ps/T(1−p)(mn−s)/T. Its normalized law is the displayed Beta distribution. Its mean tends to s/(mn) and its variance tends to zero as T↓0, including endpoint maxima. Energy for maximizing a log-likelihood is its negative; the opposite sign reverses the optimization.
Gaussian likelihood Gibbs annealing ((μn​,vn​)⟶(xˉ,S/m))
Words: 145
Likelihood-power annealing OurBigBook.com
Let xˉ=m−1∑i​xi​ and S=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2>0. With Lebesgue base measure dμdv for v=σ2, the likelihood-power law has conditionals
μ∣v∼N(xˉ,Tv/m),v∣μ∼InvGamma(2Tm​−1,2TS+m(μ−xˉ)2​).
(3)
The joint law is proper for T<m/3, since its marginal v is inverse-gamma distribution with shape m/(2T)−3/2 and scale S/(2T). There is also a direct convergence proof for successive Gibbs sampling updates with deterministic 0<Tn​≤m/10 and Tn​→0. Update μn​ from vn−1​, then vn​ from μn​. Inverse-gamma distribution moments and conditional normal moments give
Evn​=m−4Tn​S+Tn​Evn−1​​,Evn2​=(m−4Tn​)(m−6Tn​)S2+2STn​Evn−1​+3Tn2​Evn−12​​.
(4)
The coefficients of the preceding moments are bounded by 1/6 and 1/8, so these moments stay bounded from a finite deterministic initial variance. Letting Tn​→0 gives Evn​→S/m and Evn2​→(S/m)2. Also E(μn​−xˉ)2=Tn​Evn−1​/m→0. Thus the iterates converge in mean square to the normal maximum-likelihood estimate.

Local search

Words: 49
Heuristic optimization OurBigBook.com
Local search repeatedly improves a feasible solution within a specified neighborhood until no improving move remains. For an allocation, neighbors can transfer an item or exchange items between bidders while preserving the partition. A local optimum need not be a global optimum; restarting from several initial solutions can explore different basins.

Feasible point (x∈F)

Words: 69
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
A feasible point satisfies every constraint of an optimization problem. For a transportation problem with capacity inequalities, feasibility requires nonnegative shipments, row totals no greater than factory capacities and column totals equal to shop demands. Feasibility alone does not prove minimal cost: a matching transportation dual certificate with capacity inequalities provides an optimality proof. The set of all feasible points can be empty, and a finite infimum need not be attained even when the set is nonempty.

Nonlinear programming (minx​f(x) subject to gi​(x)≤0, hj​(x)=0)

Words: 53
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
A nonlinear programming problem minimizes an objective over finitely many real variables subject to constraints, with at least one objective or constraint nonlinear. Parametrizing the pulse amplitudes in quantum optimal control produces such a problem. The two spacing vectors have uniform simplex measure, independently, and the full ordered-coordinate region has volume 1/(k!)2. Simultaneous permutation of the spacing pairs preserves that measure, so all (k+1)! orders of the ratios vi​/ui​ have equal volume. Choose a nonnegative kernel vector h of minimal nonempty support inside the support of u; subtract λh, where λ=minhi​>0​ui​/hi​. The remainder is nonnegative, remains in the kernel, and has strictly smaller support. Induction proves the decomposition. On a minimal support, the kernel is one-dimensional: an independent kernel direction could perturb a strictly positive vector to the boundary of that support without making it zero, contradicting minimality. For an integer matrix with entries bounded by M, cofactor determinants give an integer generator with coordinates bounded by q!Mq, where q is the ambient number of coordinates.

Lineality space (C∩(−C))

Words: 34
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
The lineality space of a convex cone is its largest linear subspace, equal to C∩(−C). Every nonempty face contains it. A cone is pointed exactly when this space is zero.

Self-dual cone (K=K∗)

Words: 26
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
A self-dual cone equals its dual cone under the specified inner product. The nonnegative orthant, second-order cone and positive semidefinite cone are standard examples. Self-duality of a set alone does not establish primal or dual feasibility.

Proper cone

Words: 30
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
In conic optimization, a proper cone is a closed convex cone that is a pointed cone and has nonempty interior in its ambient finite-dimensional space. These conditions permit strict cone feasibility and nondegenerate barrier geometry.

Completely positive cone (CPn​)

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
The convex cone of completely positive matrices:
CPn​=cone{xxT:x∈R≥0n​}.
(38)
It is a closed convex cone and the dual cone of the copositive cone under the Frobenius inner product. The finite-sum definition imposes no closure by fiat; closedness of the completely positive cone supplies that fact.
Closedness of the completely positive cone
Words: 70
Completely positive cone OurBigBook.com
Use the conic Carathéodory theorem in the real space of symmetric matrices, of dimension N=n(n+1)/2. A convergent sequence Bℓ​ in the completely positive cone has padded factorizations Bℓ​=∑j=1N​xℓj​xℓjT​ with nonnegative factors. Their total squared norms equal trBℓ​ and are uniformly bounded. A simultaneous convergent subsequence of the finite factor tuple gives B=∑j​xj​xjT​ with xj​≥0. Thus the limit remains in the cone. The argument also bounds the required number of factors by N.

Pointed cone (K∩(−K)={0})

Words: 33
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
A convex cone containing no nonzero line through the origin, equivalently K∩(−K)={0}. The copositive cone is pointed: a matrix in both it and its negative has zero quadratic form on the nonnegative orthant; testing ei​ and ei​+ej​ kills all entries.

Closed convex cone

Words: 118 Articles: 1
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
A convex cone that is a closed set in its ambient topology. In a finite-dimensional normed vector space, this means it contains every limit of its convergent sequences. For example, the positive semidefinite cone is closed because each test X↦xTXx is continuous.
Separation from a closed convex cone
Words: 84
Closed convex cone OurBigBook.com
For a closed convex cone C in a finite-dimensional real inner product space and z∈/C, there exists y with ⟨y,z⟩<0 and ⟨y,c⟩≥0 for all c∈C. Here is a direct proof. A nearest point c0​∈C exists by compactness after restricting to a sufficiently large ball. Differentiating squared distance along the segment towards c∈C gives ⟨c0​−z,c−c0​⟩≥0. Using c=0 and c=2c0​ shows ⟨c0​−z,c0​⟩=0. Set y=c0​−z=0: then ⟨y,c⟩≥0 and ⟨y,z⟩=−∥y∥2<0. This is a conic form of the Hahn-Banach separation theorem.

Conic hull (cone(S))

Words: 150 Articles: 3
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
The set of all finite conic combinations of elements of S, including zero. It is the smallest convex cone containing S. It need not be closed even when S is closed: the closed set S={(t,1):t≥1} generates vectors converging to (1,0) via (t,1)/t, but no nonzero generated vector has second coordinate zero.
Finitely generated cone (C={∑j=1r​λj​aj​:λj​≥0})
Words: 81 Articles: 1
Conic hull OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated cone is a conic hull of a finite set of vectors. Every point admits a representation using linearly independent active generators, by eliminating dependence while keeping coefficients nonnegative.
Closedness of finitely generated cones
Words: 55
Finitely generated cone OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated cone is a closed convex cone. For a convergent sequence of represented vectors, use linearly independent active generators and pass to a subsequence with the same active set. Its coefficients converge through a fixed left inverse and retain nonnegativity. General linear images of closed cones need not be closed; finiteness of the generators supplies the missing argument.

A finite sum ∑j​λj​sj​ with λj​≥0. Unlike a convex combination, the coefficients need not sum to one. Zero coefficients and the empty sum are allowed.

Words: 176 Articles: 3
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
The real symmetric matrices that are copositive matrices form a closed convex cone:
COPn​={A:xTAx≥0 for every x∈R≥0n​}.
(39)
Each fixed x gives a closed linear inequality in A. Their intersection is therefore closed and convex, and it is preserved by nonnegative scaling.
Duality of copositive and completely positive cones (COPn∗​=CPn​)
Words: 45
Copositive cone OurBigBook.com
Under the nonnegative-pairing convention for the dual cone, CPn∗​=COPn​ follows from ⟨A,xxT⟩F​=xTAx. Conversely, if B∈/CPn​, separation from a closed convex cone gives a separating A nonnegative on all generators and negative on B. That A is a copositive matrix, so B∈/COPn∗​. This proves the displayed equality using closedness of the completely positive cone.
Interior of the copositive cone (intCOPn​)
Words: 53
Copositive cone OurBigBook.com
The interior consists exactly of strictly copositive matrices. If xTAx has positive minimum δ on the compact nonnegative unit sphere, perturbations of operator norm less than δ preserve this positive lower bound there. Conversely, if a unit nonnegative vector has zero quadratic form, A−εI leaves the copositive cone for every ε>0. Thus such a matrix is not interior. The identity matrix is a convenient interior point.
Positive-semidefinite-plus-nonnegative cone (S+n​+Nn)
Words: 40
Copositive cone OurBigBook.com
The sums P+N of a real positive semidefinite matrix P and a symmetric nonnegative matrix N form a convex cone inside the copositive cone. Both terms have nonnegative quadratic forms on the nonnegative orthant. The Horn copositive matrix shows that the inclusion is strict in dimension five; the sum of squares criterion for a biquadratic form explains this cone's relation to semidefinite programming.

Positive semidefinite cone

Words: 181 Articles: 5
Convex cone OurBigBook.com
The positive semidefinite matrices form a convex cone because nonnegative combinations preserve nonnegative quadratic forms.
Elliptope (EN​={X⪰0:diagX=1})
Words: 44
Positive semidefinite cone OurBigBook.com
The set of real positive semidefinite matrices with unit diagonal. Equivalently, its members are Gram matrices of unit vectors, by the real spectral theorem. Every two-by-two principal minor gives ∣Xij​∣≤1, so the set is bounded; it is also closed, hence compact in finite dimension. This gives attainment of linear objectives used in semidefinite programming.
Fantope (Fk​={Y:0⪯Y⪯I, trY=k})
Words: 51
Positive semidefinite cone OurBigBook.com
For an integer 0≤k≤n, the fantope is the convex hull of rank-k orthogonal projection matrices in Rn. Equivalently, it consists of real symmetric matrices with eigenvalues in [0,1] and matrix trace k. To prove the equivalence, apply the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices and express the eigenvalue vector as a convex combination of the zero-one extreme points of the capped simplex. The sum of the largest eigenvalues is its support function.

For a positive semidefinite matrix, a trace bound is a bound on the sum of its nonnegative eigenvalues.
